readerTitle: Five requests, one week: which do you act on?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 기장·회계 사무소, 지역 도매 유통사) · 모든 수치와 요청은 설명용
insight: 요청은 목소리 크기나 개수가 아니라, 그 밑에 깔린 문제를 묶어 본 뒤 가치와 비용으로 순서를 정하고, 나머지에는 대안을 붙여 '아니요'라고 말한다.
misconception: 가장 큰 고객이나 가장 최근에 요청한 고객의 말을 먼저 들어주는 것이 고객 중심이다.

sources.text: 우선순위 정하기(가치 대비 비용)와 기능 거절의 일반 원칙. 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 CUS-07-02, CUS-07-03을 적용
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(고객 수 12곳, 30곳, 8곳 등)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계로 읽히지 않도록 카드에 illustrative 라벨이 붙어 있는지 확인하세요.
도매 사례의 60일 외상 조건은 현금 흐름 부담을 설명하기 위한 일반적 예시입니다. 특정 국가의 세무·법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: Five requests, one week: which do you act on?
body: Maya runs a small bookkeeping firm with 40 small-business clients. On Monday morning she counts five different requests in her inbox and notes.
Her team has time to act on one or two this month. Every client who asked thinks their request is the obvious one.

image.label: Five sticky notes on a desk, one coffee cup
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 사무실 책상 위에 색이 다른 포스트잇 다섯 장이 흩어져 있고, 커피잔 하나와 달력. 포스트잇 글씨는 알아볼 수 없게 흐릿하게. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Where does Maya start?
list: Her **biggest client** wants a custom monthly report in its own format
**12 clients**, in different words, want faster answers to quick questions
One client wants her to run their payroll too
A prospect will sign *if* she adds weekend phone support
**6 clients** want reminders before tax deadlines

options.text: The custom report. The biggest client pays the most
options.feedback: You protect one relationship, but you spend scarce time on work only one client benefits from, while 12 others wait.

options.text: Group the requests by the problem underneath, then weigh value against effort
options.feedback: This is prioritizing what to build: count who shares the problem and what fixing it costs. It often reveals that two requests are really one.

options.text: Weekend support. Winning a new client is growth
options.feedback: New revenue matters, but you'd take on a permanent cost for one maybe-client before serving the 40 you have.

cards.title: Look under each request.
body: Two requests share one worry: *"I don't know where my books stand."* One fix, a short weekly status note with upcoming deadlines, answers both.

breakdown.label: Quick answers + deadline reminders
breakdown.detail: Same underlying problem. Low effort to fix together

breakdown.label: Custom report
breakdown.detail: One client. New work every month

breakdown.label: Payroll
breakdown.detail: A new service, not an improvement

breakdown.label: Weekend support
breakdown.detail: A prospect, not a client yet. Ongoing cost

cards.title: Prioritizing means ranking problems, not requests.
body: Customers describe solutions. Your job is to find the problem behind each one, then ask two questions: **how many customers share it**, and **what does fixing it cost**?
Maya's weekly note takes about an hour a week and calms 18 clients. The custom report would take hours every month and help one.
cards.softwareNote: In a software company these arrive as feature tickets. Three tickets asking for different exports may be one need: *get my data into my accountant's tool.* Group before you count votes.

cards.title: Now tell the biggest client.
body: The client who wants a custom report pays about a fifth of Maya's revenue. How should she answer?

options.text: Say yes. Losing them would hurt too much
options.feedback: You keep them happy today, but custom work tends to multiply. Soon each client has their own version and your team serves no one quickly.

options.text: Say no to the custom format, and offer a monthly call walking through the standard report, or custom work at a fee
options.feedback: This is saying no well: decline the request, solve the need behind it, and give a paid path if it truly matters to them.

options.text: Say "we'll look into it" and let it fade
options.feedback: It avoids an awkward moment but costs trust. A vague maybe often feels worse than a clear no with a reason.

cards.title: Counting heads isn't the whole answer.
body: A request from one client can still come first. If it protects a large share of revenue, or fixes a serious error, one voice can outweigh twelve.
And a no is usually a *not now*. Keep a short list of declined requests and look again each quarter. A request that keeps coming back from new customers is telling you something.

cards.title: Now it's a wholesale distributor.
body: You supply snacks and drinks to corner shops. This month's requests:
list: **30 shops:** move the order cut-off from 2 pm to 5 pm
**8 shops:** email invoices instead of paper
One regional chain: 60 days to pay instead of 30

options.text: Later cut-off and emailed invoices first
options.feedback: Prioritizing at work: the cut-off touches the most shops, and emailed invoices are nearly free. Big value, modest cost.

options.text: Give the chain its 60 days. It's your biggest buyer
options.feedback: You may win volume, but your cash sits with them twice as long. Saying no, or pricing the longer terms, protects the business.

options.text: Do a little of all five to keep everyone happy
options.feedback: It feels fair, but spreading thin means nothing gets done well, and each half-kept promise becomes a new complaint.

cards.softwareNote: Online stores face the same pile: a late-shipping cutoff, digital receipts, new filters. The same sort applies before anyone writes code.

cards.title: Two ideas, one pile of requests.
list: **Prioritizing what to build:** find the problem under each request, then weigh how many it helps against what it costs
**Saying no to features:** decline clearly, solve the real need another way, and offer a paid path when it fits
cards.callout: Most of the work is sorting. The no is easier once the sort is honest.
cards.softwareNote: For a product team, the sorting step is a shared list of problems, each linked to the tickets that point to it.

cards.title: Sort requests by the problem underneath, then choose.
body: The loudest or largest request is rarely the most valuable one. Group, weigh value against cost, and turn the rest into a clear, kind no.
**Try it today:** write down the last five things customers asked you for. Next to each, write the problem behind it. How many share one?
